title: At the Doctor's Office
subtitle: Three short situations: booking the appointment, saying what hurts, and understanding the pharmacist.
description: An A2 listening and reading page for one of the situations students most often have to handle alone — calling a doctor's office, describing a symptom, and following the instructions on a prescription in the United States.
source: authored for this site; no source document
passage: Three short conversations you will need sooner or later. Your lines are written out as models.
1. Booking the appointment
Receptionist: Good morning, Dr. Reed's office.
You: Good morning. I'd like to make an appointment, please.
Receptionist: Have you been here before?
You: Yes. I came in last March.
Receptionist: Could I have your date of birth?
You: June the fourth, 1992.
Receptionist: Thank you. And what's the reason for the visit?
You: I've had a sore throat for about a week, and now it hurts to swallow.
Receptionist: I can fit you in on Thursday at ten forty-five. Does that work?
You: Thursday morning is difficult. Do you have anything later in the day?
Receptionist: There's a four-fifteen on Friday.
You: Four-fifteen on Friday is perfect. Thank you.
Receptionist: Please bring your insurance card, and try to arrive ten minutes early.
2. Saying what hurts
Dr. Reed: So, what brings you in today?
You: My throat has hurt since last week. It's worse in the morning.
Dr. Reed: Have you had a fever?
You: A little on Monday. I took something for it and it went down.
Dr. Reed: Are you allergic to any medication?
You: Not that I know of.
Dr. Reed: Let me take a look. Open your mouth, please.
Dr. Reed: It's red, but it doesn't look like an infection. You should feel better in a few days.
You: Should I take anything for it?
Dr. Reed: An over-the-counter painkiller is enough. If you still feel bad on Monday, call us.
You: And can I go to work?
Dr. Reed: You can. Drink water, and rest when you get the chance.
3. At the pharmacy
Pharmacist: Can I help you?
You: Yes — I'd like to pick up a prescription. The doctor sent it over this afternoon.
Pharmacist: Date of birth, please? … Here it is. Have you taken this one before?
You: No, never.
Pharmacist: Take one tablet twice a day, with food. Don't stop early, even if you feel better.
You: How many days is it for?
Pharmacist: Ten. There's one refill on it, so if you need more, call us instead of the doctor.
You: Thank you. Is there anything I should avoid?
Pharmacist: No alcohol while you're taking it. It says so on the label too.

images.alt: A doctor sitting beside a sick child's bed in a cottage, watching her closely by lamplight
images.caption: *The Doctor* — Luke Fildes, 1891. Fildes painted it years after the death of his own son, whose doctor had kept watch beside him in the same way.

images.alt: The counter and wall of glass bottles inside a drugstore around 1900
images.caption: *Stewart's Pharmacy, Seattle* — about 1900, from the Seattle Municipal Archives. The shelves of identical glass bottles held ingredients the pharmacist measured and mixed to order.

vocabulary.definition: to arrange a fixed time to see a doctor, dentist or official
to find a free time for somebody in a full schedule
the card that shows who pays for your treatment — American offices ask for it every visit
pain in the throat, usually from a cold
to make food or drink go down your throat
sold without a prescription, straight off the shelf
to go somewhere and collect it
a small hard piece of medicine you swallow — careful: not a computer
permission to collect the same prescription again without seeing the doctor

exercises.title: Saying It the Natural Way
exercises.instructions: Choose the form an American receptionist, doctor or pharmacist would expect.

items.prompt: You call the office. You say:
options: I'd like to make an appointment.
I want to mark an hour.
I need to take an hour.
items.explanation: You make an appointment in English. "Mark an hour" translates directly from other languages and will not be understood.

items.prompt: The doctor asks "What brings you in today?" This means:
items.explanation: "What brings you in?" is the normal, friendly way of asking what the problem is.

items.prompt: Complete: "I've had a sore throat ___ a week."
items.explanation: A length of time takes "for": for a week. "Since" takes a starting point: since Monday.

items.prompt: A painkiller you can buy with no prescription is:
items.explanation: Over-the-counter medicine sits on the shelf. "Under the counter" means sold illegally.

items.prompt: The receptionist offers Thursday. You cannot come. The most polite reply is:
options: Thursday is difficult. Do you have anything later?
Thursday is bad for me, change it.
items.explanation: English softens a refusal: say it is "difficult" and ask a question, rather than giving an order.

items.prompt: "There's one refill on it" means you can:
options: collect the same medicine once more
pay for it in two parts
return it if it does not work
items.explanation: A refill is permission to collect the prescription again without going back to the doctor.

exercises.title: At the Office and the Pharmacy

items.prompt: Please bring your insurance ___ to every visit.
items.explanation: It is an insurance card in American English.

items.prompt: I can ___ you in on Friday afternoon.
items.explanation: To fit somebody in is to find them a free time in a full day.

items.prompt: It hurts to ___ , so I am drinking very slowly.
items.explanation: Swallowing is what makes a sore throat hurt most.

items.prompt: I came to ___ up a prescription.
items.explanation: You pick up a prescription at the pharmacy.

items.prompt: Take one ___ twice a day, with food.
items.explanation: A tablet is the small hard piece of medicine. In Portuguese a tablet is a computer — here it is a pill.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the conversations.

items.statement: The appointment is finally on Thursday morning.
items.explanation: False — Thursday was difficult, so the appointment is at four-fifteen on Friday.

items.statement: The doctor thinks the throat is infected.
items.explanation: False — "It's red, but it doesn't look like an infection."

items.statement: The doctor says you may go to work.
items.explanation: True — "You can. Drink water, and rest when you get the chance."

items.statement: You should stop the medicine as soon as you feel better.
items.explanation: False — the pharmacist says "Don't stop early, even if you feel better."

items.statement: You should not drink alcohol while taking the medicine.
items.explanation: True — "No alcohol while you're taking it. It says so on the label too."

discussion: Role-play situation 1: one of you is the receptionist and has no free time before next week.
How do you describe pain in your own language? Do you say "my throat hurts" or "I have pain in the throat"?
The doctor asks three questions before looking at your throat. What are they, and why does she ask them first?
Write a short dialogue (about eight lines) at a pharmacy where the medicine the doctor ordered is out of stock.
